items.title: Ramaphosa rejects claims ANC plans to use asylum seekers in elections
items.summary: African National Congress (ANC) President Cyril Ramaphosa has rubbished claims that the party has brought in asylum seekers to bolster its support at the local government elections as fake news. Speaking during the Black Wednesday Commemoration that took place today in Sandton, Ramaphosa cautioned against the spread of disinformation and fake news. He used the event to engage with journalists and editors from various media houses. A fake news post has been circulating on social media claiming that asylum seekers are being registered to vote and, in turn, will vote for the ANC. Ramaphosa says such posts are fake. “There’s just no way that the ANC would get asylum seekers to vote for it. There’s just no way. It’s a rubbish story. It does not exist. We never want to do something like that, and (it just shows you) the dangers of these social media platforms, where the story is planted by an individual who is not accountable to anyone and it starts spreading,” says Ramaphosa.

items.originalTitle: Journalists’ body warns Trump’s crackdown threatens press freedom
items.author: Nomcebo Miya
items.title: Journalists’ body warns Trump’s crackdown threatens press freedom
items.summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an international New York-based press-freedom organisation, has warned that the Trump administration’s restrictions on the media are emboldening authoritarian governments around the world. Speaking to the SABC News as South Africa marks Black Wednesday, CPJ’s Americas director, José Zamora, accused Washington of making independent reporting more dangerous and costly through restrictions on access, legal pressure and immigration measures targeting journalists. Zamora says the consequences extend beyond newsrooms, weakening the public’s ability to expose abuses and hold those in power accountable. Since President Trump’s first term in office, he’s had a tempestuous relationship with the press. In September, after the White House sought to bar certain U.S. media from its grounds , this was an exchange in the Oval Office. “Are you trying to intimidate the press from doing their job,” asks Sherwin Bryce-Pease. “No no no no. I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you’re terrible but I dislike dishonest, I like to see honest press,” replies Trump. Or this response from President Trump, when a journalist challenged him on the war in Iran; “I had total military victory, but the fake news, guys like you, write incorrectly. You’re a fake guy, guys like you write about it incorrectly. We had a total military victory,” says Trump. Or here hinting that they might bar legacy publications from the White House as well. “The New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news, they’re crummy papers… we haven’t taken the step of throwing them out. But they’re fake news,” he says. As CPJ raises concerns of democratic backsliding in the USA, the group’s Regional Director for the Americas, Jose Zamora “It is a global issue. We are seeing a democratic backsliding and authoritarian regression. And the US, sadly, is a it’s a leader in that movement. I think we should remember Black Wednesday as a warning when governments silence those who expose abuses, they make further abuses easier to hide. And I think Black Wednesday really reminds us of why governments target journalists. Independent reporting exposes abuses of power. And that that is what we are seeing today in the United States,” says Zamora. Actions taken by the Trump administration against the press includes removing funding for public broadcasting; exclusion of media houses from the White House over editorial decisions or coverage deemed too negative; the Pentagon introduced rules restricting reporters from seeking information not authorised for release, including unclassified material -major news organisations surrendered their credentials in protest; or using regulatory power against broadcasters over editorial decisions it does not agree with. Federal courts have intervened to restore White House access for several news organisations , finding that their exclusion likely violated constitutional protections for free expression and due process but those protections remain subject to ongoing litigation and appeals. Additionally, the Trump administration says its decisions are intended to cut spending, address alleged political bias and protect national security. It argues taxpayers should not fund partisan broadcasting, describes presidential access as a privilege it can control, and defends Pentagon restrictions as necessary to protect sensitive information. It also presents regulatory investigations as efforts to hold broadcasters accountable for alleged news distortion. Zamora argues that some of these actions are in violation of the law. “The US was a leader in promoting press freedom, human rights, fighting corruption and upholding transparency. Now, when other regions of the world that are more susceptible to these kinds of environments see that a country where democracy was once strongly protected is doing this, it emboldens them to become authoritarian and abusive,” he adds. And while the Trump administration argues that its the most transparent in American history, CPJ presents a different assessment. “Based on everything that we have documented and the patterns that we’ve seen at CPJ, that’s not true. It’s not the most open and it’s actually the most repressive. They’ve done everything within their power to harass the press, to create a very hostile environment for the press,” says Zamora. The 2026 World Press Freedom Index, released in April, ranked the United States 64th out of 180 countries, it’s lowest ranking on record. As Black Wednesday offers us a poignant reminder of the cost of silencing the press and the solidarity needed to defend it. items.title: Masemola must restore confidence in police: Public Interest SA
items.summary: Non-profit organisation Public Interest SA says there are now expectations for National Police Commissioner Fannie Masemola to eliminate corruption and wrongdoing in the police force. Masemola returned to office today after President Cyril Ramaphosa lifted his precautionary suspension last Friday. Ramaphosa’s decision came after the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) withdrew all criminal charges against him relating to the alleged contravention of the Public Finance Management Act. The organisation’s founder Tebogo Khaas says Masemola must ensure that public confidence in the police is restored. “For us, it is a welcome relief to have General Masemola back; however, as he mentioned in his statement, the president said he must go and clean up the South African Police Service, and we expect him to do that and nothing less. And cleaning SAPS means making uncomfortable decisions or actions must be taken against anyone and everyone who has been pointed to have done anything wrong or improperly.” Meanwhile, Masemola says he is not returning to work to seek revenge against anyone. Instead, his priorities, he says, will be stabilising and uniting the SAPS.

items.originalTitle: Majodina says tests show no cholera in Tshwane patients
items.author: Baphelele Malindisa
items.title: Majodina says tests show no cholera in Tshwane patients
items.summary: Water and Sanitation Minister Pemmy Majodina says tests conducted on patients infected with a gastrointestinal illness in the City of Tshwane found no traces of cholera. She says, however, high levels of E.coli have been found in the water emanating from the Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Plant, which was not chlorinated between the 24th of September and the 14th of this month. This as over 400 cases of gastrointestinal illnesses have been reported in Tshwane’s Region 7 since the beginning of October. Majodina says a response team has been established to conduct additional tests and investigations into the matter. “Laboratory test results from stool specimens from infected patients by the NICD coupled with the tests of water emanating from the Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Works, indicated that illness has been caused by residents being exposed to contaminated water from this water treatment plant. No cholera bacteria were found in the sampled stools,” says Majodina. Affected communities include Zithobeni, Bronkhorstspruit, Dark City, Rethabiseng and Sokhulumi, which are largely supplied by the City of Tshwane’s Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Works. Residents in Bronkhorstspruit have been urged not to use tap water for drinking or cooking, due to a water quality and public health crisis. Health Department outlines measures to protect communities: Tshwane Executive Mayor Nasiphi Moya warned that tap water does not meet drinking standards and has advised communities not to use it for purposes other than flushing toilets, while water tankers continue supplying affected areas. Moya noted that the situation is reminiscent of last year’s typhoid outbreak in Hammanskraal, which required cooperation between different government departments. The mayor further highlighted that water delivered by tankers is routinely tested to ensure it’s safe for drinking. “ We had a similar situation last year in H amanskraal when we were dealing with typhoid cases, and we tried as much as possible, working with different spheres of government and different departments, to make sure that the situation doesn’t get worse. The investment has been made in terms of what needs to happen, because, as the minister was saying, the source is in the water … t here’s no going about it. We need to resolve the issue of clean water in B ronkhorstspruit,” says Moya. “Once we restore water to the people of B ronkhorstspruit , as government, I think that’s what we need to do, in the short term, we are obviously taking heed and counsel from the relevant departments and entities that says the people of B ronkhorstspruit must not use the water beyond, you know, just flushing with the water that’s coming out of the plant, that the people of Bronkhorstspruit we’ll continue to supply them with tankers. Those tankers are routinely being tested to make sure that the water that we deliver to them in the tank is clean and is drinkable,” she adds. items.originalTitle: Rain-hit Proteas lose three wickets on second day of second Test
items.author: Thabiso Malesele
items.title: Rain-hit Proteas lose three wickets on second day of second Test
items.summary: Most of the second day of the second Test match between South Africa and Australia was lost due to inclement weather and a wet outfield. Play eventually got underway in a truncated evening session, where just over 31 overs were bowled. The South Africans added 77 runs to their total but lost three wickets. The hosts were on 97 for the loss of five wickets at stumps. South Africa resumed their first innings on 20 for the loss of two wickets late in the afternoon on day two at St George’s Park after most of the day was lost to persistent rain and then a wet outfield. Captain Temba Bavuma was unbeaten on four, and Marques Ackerman, making his Test debut, was on five. Sadly, for Proteas fans and Ackerman, his innings didn’t last much longer. Seamer Scott Boland claimed his third scalp of the match, removing the debutant for six in his second over. And it only got worse for the hosts as quick Mitchell Starc also got in on the wickets, dismissing Mathew Breetzke for four, leaving them reeling on 40 for four. Staying composed under pressure and finding some consistency Bavuma and Ryan Rickleton steadied the innings with a 52-run fifth-wicket partnership. But Boland, the destroyer-in-chief broke through claiming his fourth wicket as he accounted for Rickleton for 31. Bavuma was unbeaten on 41 and Wiaan Mulder on 2 as the Proteas ended the day on 97 for the loss of five wickets.

items.originalTitle: ACCOUNTABILITY DIVIDE OP-ED: SA and Kazakhstan reveal sharply contrasting paths to biological weapons dismantlement
items.author: Andrea Uhlig, Wilmot James and Brendan Beng
items.title: ACCOUNTABILITY DIVIDE OP-ED: SA and Kazakhstan reveal sharply contrasting paths to biological weapons dismantlement
items.summary: South Africa’s apartheid-era Project Coast biological weapons programme was dismantled in the 1990s with limited transparency, external oversight and accountability, leaving unresolved concerns about materials, records and expertise. In contrast, Kazakhstan’s more transparent, internationally supervised dismantlement highlights the importance of verification, institutional safeguards and redirecting former weapons scientists towards peaceful research to prevent proliferation.

items.title: Five police officers arrested at the Polokwane International Airport
items.summary: Five police officers stationed at the Polokwane International Airport have been arrested in connection with corruption and defeating the ends of justice. Following the arrests, the Limpopo Police Commissioner, Jan Scheepers, again emphasised the province’s zero tolerance policy for crime committed by police officers. The officers are expected to appear in court tomorrow. Scheepers says it’s sad to see young SAPS being involved in acts of criminality. “It’s sad that we see our young members doing corruption and not honouring the badge and not honouring the organization and not honouring our communities. They thought we made a joke when we said we will change blue uniforms for an orange one. It was not a joke. In this province, we are dedicated, together with my whole management team. If you are corrupt and you’re wearing the blue uniform, we will change it to an orange one. That’s it,” says Scheepers. “It’s a sad day when we see young people with a bright future in front of them doing criminal activities, but you cannot fight crime when you have criminals in your own rank. It cannot happen,” he adds.

items.originalTitle: Expert believes Tembe was possibly pushed from balcony
items.author: Paballo Lephaka
items.title: Expert believes Tembe was possibly pushed from balcony
items.summary: A forensic evidence expert in the Anele Tembe inquest has raised questions about the circumstances surrounding her death. Lieutenant-Colonel Jeremy Philander says he believes Tembe was possibly pushed from the balcony of a Cape Town. It’s alleged she fell from the balcony while with rapper Kiernan Forbes in April 2021. Philander says, “The physical evidence is not consistent with the possibility that the deceased slipped and fell from the balcony. The time it took for the body to fall ranges between 2.3 and 2.6 seconds. The absolute minimum impact velocity was calculated at 82 kilometres per hour, a velocity high enough to cause serious damage to the human body and most likely death.” Tony Forbes, the father of the late rapper Kiernan “AKA” Forbes, says he is patient with the legal process and pleased that the inquest has finally started after five years. Tembe, who was engaged to AKA, died after falling from the tenth floor of a Cape Town hotel in April 2021. Forbes says he is willing to remain patient as he wants justice to take its course. “I’m happy that the inquest is resuming. Um, it’s been five years since the incident. So, I think it’s good that, you know, finally, the inquest is gaining momentum. So, I’m happy to be here and observe and listen and understand,” he says.

More than 400 cases of gastrointestinal illness have been reported in the area since early this month. Most of those affected are under the age of four. Now the city is working on increasing the supply of clean drinking water to affected communities. This includes the deployment of a total of 36 water tankers. Water and Sanitation Minister, Pemmy Majodina, revealed this at a meeting on Monday. items.summary: The Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies, Solly Malatsi, says the government is working to ensure that learners from disadvantaged communities enjoy equal digital opportunities. He was speaking at the launch of a mobile digital laboratory at the Fontein Full-Service School in Nelson Mandela Bay, in the Eastern Cape. The lab will benefit more than 800 learners with basic computer skills and also assist teachers with the integration of technology in the classroom. The venture is a public-private partnership, and Malatsi says a collaborative effort is essential to address digital inequalities. The Eastern Cape has more than 5,000 public schools, and a substantial number of these schools are without IT facilities. This leaves thousands of learners unable to access the digital space. Fontein Primary School was identified as one of the schools that required access to E-learning. This lab is a public-private partnership collaboration. Minister Malatsi says collaborations are the best way forward to equip schools. CYBER LAB LAUNCH | 19 October 2026 The Principal of Fontein Primary School, Gary Groenewald, together with Sanders Hansa, a teacher at the school and leader of the Cyber Lab project, expressed their excitement about this exciting opportunity for learners. https://t.co/4oRCJvfNPK — Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality (@NMandelaBaymuni) October 19, 2026 “We also need municipalities to come to the party. We need provincial governments and the Departments of Education in these provinces to ensure that the connectivity provided to the schools is also of the level of quality, that can cope with the size of the school, you would find that in most instances, the school’s rollout program provides 10 megabytes per second. That is slow when you look at the connectivity that is in here. And it’s a point that we are emphasising with the schools. The schools, the Department of Education, together with the provincial government, are responsible for ensuring that the network is available in the school,” says Malatsi. The CEO of Cassava Technologies, Ziaad Suleman, says this investment was made to empower the learners, taking them into the digital age. “The types of skills that they learn is everything from soft skills, including the digital skills around basic computer literacy, coding, and a whole lot of other things that will actually allow them to start at a base, but then elevate themselves. In terms of the investment, it is multifaceted, because it’s not only about the building of the actual building itself. It costs in the region of between R3m and R5m, but ultimately, what it does is that for us, it gives purpose and the cost is immeasurable,” says Suleman. A lot of them are already excited seeing the lab standing in front of our classroom and they are so stoked for the journey that’s coming with the teachers. Teachers will be able to use the lab to incorporate technology into their lessons as well,” says Hansa. items.originalTitle: UN climate panel head wants swift end to deadlock over key scientific report
items.author: Estelle.Bronkhorst
items.title: UN climate panel head wants swift end to deadlock over key scientific report
items.summary: UN climate panel head wants swift end to deadlock over key scientific report Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 18:30 GENEVA - The world's top climate scientists will reconvene at the earliest opportunity, the panel's chair said on Monday, after member states failed to agree when to release its crucial new findings on global heating. The IPCC, a United Nations body, is the global authority on climate science. Its reports bring together the latest knowledge on climate change, its causes, potential impacts and options for responding. They are the key reference point for international agreements on how to tackle the climate crisis, are used by governments to develop national climate policies and have been quoted in international court rulings. The IPCC suspended its latest negotiations late on Friday after a week of tough talks in the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa. Many of the IPCC's nearly 200 member countries want its next major report out in time for a crucial United Nations climate summit in 2028. That summit is due to take stock of the world's progress so far in cutting planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions and is a key decision-making point. But some IPCC members -- including Saudi Arabia, India and China -- have argued that more time is needed to incorporate science and data from developing nations and have said the new report should be delayed until 2029. "Reaching consensus on the schedule for our upcoming IPCC reports is vital," IPCC chair Jim Skea said on Monday. "Our reports... help communicate the scale of climate risks and the urgency of mitigation, adaptation and international cooperation." - Best available evidence - Skea said that because the Addis Ababa meeting ran past the closing time, many countries -- notably smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change -- had to leave. He said it was essential for all countries in the IPCC to be able fully to participate in the negotiations to ensure the body's assessments on the state of the planet were "robust, representative and responsive to the needs of all countries". The IPCC, set up in 1988, knits together assessments from thousands of climate scientists who work voluntarily to compile its mammoth reports. They are normally released every five to seven years. The most recent came out in 2021. Skea said the meeting in Addis Ababa had agreed on many issues, including on artificial intelligence. But member governments had not yet reached consensus on a timeline for completing the next report "and the IPCC budget that will support our work". "I will reconvene this plenary session at the earliest opportunity so the panel can effectively conclude its business," he said. Some 117 scientists working on the new report signed an open letter saying: "Our message to governments and to the world is simple: we will keep working." The world's response to "the urgency of the climate crisis" must be guided by the best available evidence, said the letter, seen by AFP. "An assessment that arrives after the decisions it is meant to inform cannot serve its purpose," it insisted. "The second Global Stocktake in 2028 is such a decision point -- and the world should not have to face it without the IPCC's latest assessment." AFP

items.summary: Indonesian stocks hit six-year low as downgrade looms Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 18:30 JAKARTA - The main stock index in Jakarta closed at its lowest level in six years on Monday, following sharp losses last week, as index compiler MSCI considers stripping Indonesia of its emerging market status. The Southeast Asian nation's benchmark Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) fell 3.6 percent to close at 4,996, a level last seen in 2020. It was the second consecutive day of heavy losses after the JCI plunged more than 11 percent on Friday in the biggest single-day fall since early 1998. The index has plummeted more than 40 percent since the start of the year. The MSCI said on Friday it was it was "no longer appropriate" to maintain Indonesia's emerging-market status and was considering whether to reclassify it as a "Standalone Market". The US firm cited a lack of progress on investors' concerns over "ongoing opacity in shareholding structures", as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information. The reclassification could trigger passive funds outflows worth $5.6 billion from Indonesia, according to Goldman Sachs. It would also put Indonesia in the same bracket as countries such as Argentina, Ukraine and Bulgaria. Monday's decline suggested that investors are still looking at an "adjustment of risk premiums", Bank Danamon Indonesia economist Irman Faiz told AFP. "Looking ahead, volatility is expected to remain high and, while a technical rebound is possible, low valuations do not guarantee a sustained recovery," Irman said. "The key lies in demonstrable improvements in transparency and regulatory enforcement, alongside stability in the Indonesian rupiah." AFP

items.title: 'Physical hell': Hong Kong hosts gruelling underwater hockey tournament
items.summary: 'Physical hell': Hong Kong hosts gruelling underwater hockey tournament Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 18:30 HONG KONG - Swimmers brandishing short, curved sticks held their breath as they somersaulted and dove towards a weighted puck at the bottom of a Hong Kong swimming pool, vying for first place in a sport likened to voluntary drowning. The annual underwater hockey tournament, ominously advertised as "physical hell", nevertheless drew a roster of hardcore enthusiasts from countries across Asia to the Chinese city over the weekend. "You have to choose when to use your breath and when not to... Anyone that's got the puck, you know that they've got some level of suffering," Leo Lines, a Japanese-New Zealander competitor from Hokkaido, told AFP. "I love that." Suited up in snorkel masks and fins, players only resurface for air when they absolutely have to, and their heads remain constantly underwater so they can monitor the game. There are six players on each team and no goalkeepers, while referees watch for fouls and send players to a penalty box for serious rule-breaking. AFP | Flora BRADLEY-WATSON "You're so into trying to succeed, trying to score the goal, that you forget about breath-holding and how tough it is," competitor Rita Frieske, a Hong Kong-based Polish academic, told AFP. Games last 30 minutes and are split into two halves with a three-minute break in between. The gruelling sport has created a tight-knit community. "It's like that sadistic study that forces everybody to survive together and then you stick together for a long time," Malaysian player Hui Chin Teoh said. Underwater hockey, previously known as "octopush", was invented in England in 1954 as a way to keep divers fit during the off-season winter months. While not yet an Olympic sport, it is recognised by the International Olympic Committee, and made its debut at the Southeast Asian Games in 2019. Competition organisers hope that as underwater camera technology improves, the spectator experience will too. "The future of underwater hockey, thanks to social media, is more active now than before," said head coach and tournament director Nowie Ignacio. "When I was playing, it was just word of mouth. Now there are a lot of avenues to see it... (competitions) are actually televised live now," he said. Many players at the Hong Kong tournament have their sights set on the Elite world championship in France next April, which organisers expect will draw around 20 nations. "People are starting to understand what underwater hockey is," Ignacio said. "The dream is the Olympics." by Flora Bradley-watson (AFP)

items.title: Number Of The Day | 43% | 19 October 2026
items.summary: Number Of The Day | 43% | 19 October 2026 Vusi.Bafetane Mon, 10/19/2026 - 17:31 When Petrol Becomes an Economic Trap: South Africa's Shrinking Room to Move Fuel-price shocks do more than raise the cost of a journey. They can gradually strip households, businesses and government of the flexibility needed to recover. There is a moment when a petrol-price increase stops being a transport story and becomes a question about the country's economic resilience. South Africa may be approaching that point. In the latest comparison discussed on eNCA's Number of the Day, the Gauteng price of 95 unleaded petrol had risen from R21.12 in November 2025 to R30.25 in October 2026, an increase of approximately 43%. The immediate pressure is obvious at the filling station. The more difficult problem is what happens after the driver leaves the forecourt. A sustained fuel-price shock travels through an economy, affecting the cost of moving goods, providing services, operating businesses and maintaining household budgets. Each additional expense leaves less money available for something else. The economy loses flexibility before it loses momentum Consider a household managing a fixed monthly income. A higher petrol bill may initially appear manageable. The family reduces discretionary spending, delays a purchase or adjusts its travel routine. But if food and transport costs rise together, those small adjustments begin to compete with essential spending. Businesses face a related dilemma. A delivery company can absorb additional fuel costs for a limited period, increase its prices or reduce activity. None of those decisions is painless. Absorbing costs reduces profitability. Increasing prices transfers pressure to customers. Cutting activity can limit employment and expansion. The cumulative result is an economy in which more people are trying to protect existing spending rather than creating new demand. Fuel becomes a constraint on economic choice, even for people who do not own vehicles. Why one price increase can trigger another Fuel costs also complicate monetary policy. When higher transport and production costs contribute to persistent inflation, the South African Reserve Bank faces a difficult balancing act: restraining price pressures without adding unnecessary strain to an already vulnerable economy. Higher interest rates can help contain broader inflationary demand, but they do not directly reverse an international oil-price shock. That creates an uncomfortable mismatch. Households can face higher fuel costs while also paying more to service debt. The deeper economic loss lies in the reversal of expectations. When households and businesses plan around the prospect of lower borrowing costs, a sudden change in the inflation outlook can interrupt investment, consumption and financial recovery. For South Africa, where economic growth and household affordability remain central concerns, that reversal deserves as much attention as the petrol-price increase itself. Government faces the same squeeze The state has its own version of this problem. A weaker economic outlook can increase pressure on public finances precisely when citizens and businesses need support. Reducing fuel-related levies may offer some relief to consumers, but it also raises questions about government revenue and how any shortfall would be managed. Allowing borrowing to expand can preserve spending temporarily, yet additional debt creates future financing obligations. This is where fiscal credibility becomes important. A government that spends more servicing debt has less room to fund infrastructure, education and other priorities without raising revenue or reallocating expenditure. The Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement is therefore more than an accounting exercise. It offers an opportunity to demonstrate whether government can maintain a credible financial path despite an adverse economic environment. Resilience requires more than waiting for relief South Africa cannot determine global oil prices. It can, however, examine how exposed its households, logistics systems and public finances are to volatility. Greater transparency around fuel-price components, more reliable transport alternatives, better infrastructure and disciplined fiscal planning all speak to the same underlying question: how can the country reduce the damage caused by the next external shock? The objective should not simply be to return to a cheaper litre of petrol. It should be to build an economy in which one unpredictable expense does not force millions of difficult decisions elsewhere. A resilient economy is not one that never experiences shocks. It is one that retains enough room to respond when they arrive. Reference · eNCA, Number of the Day, 19 October 2026. items.originalTitle: Indonesia fires have burned nearly two million hectares: monitor
items.author: Estelle.Bronkhorst
items.title: Indonesia fires have burned nearly two million hectares: monitor
items.summary: Indonesia fires have burned nearly two million hectares: monitor Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 16:30 JAKARTA - Fires in Indonesia that have caused a regional haze crisis burned through over 1.9 million hectares between January and the end of September this year, a monitor analysing satellite imagery said on Monday. The new figures came as Indonesian officials rebuffed calls to declare the fires a national disaster and said the country was "still capable of handling the situation ourselves" after neighbouring Malaysia again offered assistance. New figures from deforestation monitoring site Nusantara Atlas showed an area nearly 12 times larger than London has burned this year in Indonesia, the bulk of it as drought took hold from June, exacerbated by a strong El Niño cycle. Indonesia's government has not provided official figures for areas burned since announcing 202,000 hectares had been razed by the end of July. Nusantara Atlas founder David Gaveau said the true scale of the burning was likely to be even higher than the 1,916,588 hectares his organisation has detected so far. "Our burned-area estimates are conservative for two reasons. First, we exclude individual burn scars smaller than 6.25 hectares... Second, we prioritise avoiding false detections," he said. This year, the calculation has also been impacted by heavy haze, which has obscured satellite images at times. "The total reported burned area therefore underestimates the true area burned," he said. Even so, Nusantara Atlas data shows the area burned by the end of September this year was 38 percent higher than the same point in 2019. The satellites the monitor uses were not available during severe fires in 2015, so comparable data is not available. But Gaveau said it was likely this year would be similarly bad. "My intuition is that it probably is as bad. If you look at the sheer number of hotspots, it's still trending up and up," he said. Indonesia's forestry ministry did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment on the figures. - 'We are still capable' - Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe, sickening hundreds of thousands of people locally and spiking air pollution in neighbouring countries. The haze has prompted school closures in Malaysia and East Timor, with haze drifting into Singapore and as far afield as the Philippines. AFP | Mohd Rasfan Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) confirmed Monday that the number of consecutive days in which air quality dipped into "unhealthy" levels has surpassed that of 2015, when the region experienced its worst haze crisis. By Monday, there had been 15 consecutive days classed as "unhealthy" based on the local PSI air quality measuring system, exceeding the eight measured in 2015, NEA deputy director Jason Evan Tan told AFP. Singapore classes a day as "unhealthy" if the local PSI measure tips over 100 at any point during the day. A separate analysis by AFP data journalists showed Monday was the 15th consecutive day on which the average PSI across Singapore hit over 100 at any hour of the day, though overall haze levels were lower than last week. Singapore sent warnings to three more companies on Monday, urging them to take action against the fires, the NEA said. It followed notices sent to seven other Indonesian companies on Friday, telling them to deploy fire-fighting teams, stop burning or starting new fires, and submit their action plans to the NEA. "Since then, there are indications that smoke from fires in Kalimantan on lands held via concessions under three additional companies in Indonesia could have moved to Singapore," the NEA said in a statement. Indonesia insisted Monday it did not need foreign help fighting the blazes. "It is not a question of whether assistance is available," said Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs, Dudung Abdurachman "For the time being, however, we are still capable of handling the situation ourselves." "Then, if something happens and we need a different plan or a different nine, we will see," the Italian added. But their impressive start to the campaign is taking place against the backdrop of being found guity of more than 100 charges of breaching financial rules in English football's top flight -- all of which City deny, with Maresca having repeatedly insisted he "trusts the club completely". items.author: Estelle.Bronkhorst
items.title: 'I call it a bribe': Pennsylvania residents spurn $10,000 data centre checks
items.summary: 'I call it a bribe': Pennsylvania residents spurn $10,000 data centre checks Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 10:30 HAZLE TOWNSHIP - On his terrace overlooking the forest in eastern Pennsylvania, Ed Negra lays out four letters. All are from a developer promising a $10,000 check to each household once its data centre is running. "I call it a bribe," says the American retiree. The scene is picture-perfect. Autumn leaves are turning russet, and there is a stunning mountain view in this corner of Pennsylvania, a key state in America's upcoming midterm elections. "We thought it was a beautiful place to retire," says the septuagenarian, who used to manage a large building-supply store in neighbouring New Jersey. He and his wife settled in a sprawling gated community with round-the-clock security. Eagle Rock Resort, in Hazle Township, has hundreds of comfortable homes scattered through the woods, two golf courses, swimming pools, an equestrian centre, and even a few ski slopes for the winter. "We didn't know until we heard all the noise" of chainsaws in late 2024, Negra recalls. More than 500 hectares of land below the resort were cleared to build the future server complex. AFP | Matthew Hatcher Residents quickly mobilised. They were furious that no one had warned them, and they worried about noise and pollution. Their fight echoes many conflicts across the United States over data centres, which have become an issue in the November 3 vote. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data centre projects in the first three months of 2026, according to Data Center Watch, which tracks resistance to the industry. And polls show that the hostility crosses party lines. But Republican President Donald Trump fervently backs these projects in the name of US dominance in artificial intelligence, and he chastises those who oppose them. - 'Drop in the bucket' - In Hazle Township, residents won a court-ordered halt to construction as well as a municipal moratorium. AFP | Matthew Hatcher A few pieces of heavy equipment sit idle on the vast cleared tract. The logs have already been hauled away. But developer NorthPoint Development has not given up. Its letters now flood local mailboxes, saying "there is a lot of misinformation and fear that has circulated about data centres and our project." The letters also lay out a $165 million fund for the township and its residents. The money would pay for a new police station, lower trash fees and more. Part of it, $45 million, is to be paid directly to the 4,500 households once the data centre's first building goes into service. In the former mining town, one in six residents lives below the poverty line, according to official data. "For a young, struggling couple... living from paycheck to paycheck, $10,000 is a lot of money," says Jeff Fasnacht, a retired high school teacher who lives in the gated community. Like Negra, he sees the offer as a bribe. He also calls it "a drop in the bucket" compared with how much value his home could lose if the project goes ahead. "This was supposed to be pristine forest forever," sighs the golf enthusiast. Neither the developer nor township officials responded to AFP's requests for comment. - 'David and Goliath' - Across the valley, residents of rural Sugarloaf Township are fighting a high-voltage power line that is likely intended to supply the data centre. They are not eligible for the possible $10,000 check. "There's no amount of money that can replace or take away the beauty, the tranquillity that we live in," says Annie Vinatieri. She shares a house with her in-laws, her husband and their young son. She has been fighting the power line for almost two years. "This fight feels akin to a David and Goliath fight," she says. She takes heart in how many residents have rallied against tech interests: "The empowerment is unbelievable." AFP | Matthew Hatcher Erika Cook lives nearby and works remotely for an insurance company. She and her husband raise a few chickens and keep a vegetable garden. They also tap maple trees for syrup in the woods on their property. Part of that land is now the target of an eminent domain proceeding to make room for a huge transmission tower. Republicans dominate at the ballot box in this region. Cook says opposition to data centres has one virtue here: "It's bringing people together... across party lines." by Myriam Lemetayer

items.originalTitle: Faith and fury: Texas Senate rivals offer contrasting visions
items.author: Estelle.Bronkhorst
items.title: Faith and fury: Texas Senate rivals offer contrasting visions
items.summary: Faith and fury: Texas Senate rivals offer contrasting visions Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 10:30 DALLAS - One preaches love and reconciliation. The other champions confrontation and unyielding conservatism. Both invoke Christianity as they battle for a US Senate seat in Texas that could help determine control of Congress. Democrat James Talarico, a 37-year-old former teacher and aspiring Presbyterian minister, faces Republican Ken Paxton, a 63-year-old political survivor whose loyalty to President Donald Trump has helped him overcome years of scandal. Their contest on November 3 has become unexpectedly competitive in a state where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994, presenting voters with two sharply contrasting political figures. AFP/File | RONALDO SCHEMIDT - James Talarico: 'Politics of love' - As a child at his church's daycare center, James Talarico would intervene to break up fights, according to the pastor who has known him since infancy. Jim Rigby, who baptised Talarico and married his parents, remembers the youngster as a "calming presence." Decades later, that temperament has become central to the Democrat's appeal. A former middle school teacher and nonprofit director, Talarico was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2018 and has built a national following with speeches that fuse progressive politics, biblical teachings and criticism of America's wealthy elites. "I'll always put Texas before any political party," he has declared. A Presbyterian seminarian, Talarico draws inspiration from Jesus's commandment to love one's neighbour, arguing that faith demands compassion for the poor, immigrants and marginalised communities. He has challenged conservative Christians on their own theological ground, condemning Christian nationalism and opposing government-sponsored religious displays in public schools. His political message combines support for abortion rights and greater economic equality with appeals to voters weary of partisan hostility. Talarico's conversational style and command of scripture have generated viral social media clips, while a two-hour appearance on comedian Joe Rogan's hugely popular podcast in 2025 introduced him to an audience beyond traditional Democratic circles. But his progressive theology has provoked fierce criticism from religious conservatives, particularly over his positions on abortion and LGBTQ rights. His suggestion that God is "nonbinary" drew accusations of blasphemy, while his more cautious recent language on transgender issues has raised questions among some of his own supporters. Talarico has sought to broaden his appeal by defending Texas's oil industry and criticising aspects of former president Joe Biden's immigration policies. He defeated the more combative congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary, promising a "politics of love." POOL/AFP/File | SAUL LOEB - Ken Paxton: The MAGA survivor - Ken Paxton's political career has repeatedly appeared close to collapse. Yet the Texas attorney general has survived criminal charges, impeachment and years of damaging revelations to emerge as one of the most recognisable champions of Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement. A lawyer educated at Baylor University and the University of Virginia, Paxton entered the Texas legislature in 2003 and made his name challenging the Republican establishment from the right. He became attorney general in 2015, turning the office into a formidable legal weapon against Democratic administrations and progressive causes. His lawsuits targeting immigration policies, abortion access, environmental regulations and the Biden administration made him a hero to grassroots conservatives. Paxton also supported Trump's attempts to overturn his 2020 election defeat, cementing his standing with the president's most loyal supporters. Like Talarico, Paxton places religion at the centre of his politics, but he champions a different vision of Christianity, one that emphasises traditional morality and the defense of a nation he believes was founded on biblical principles. "In Texas classrooms, we want the Word of God opened, the Ten Commandments displayed and prayers lifted up," he declared in 2025. His political resilience has nevertheless been tested by repeated scandals. In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House impeached him over allegations of corruption and abuse of power, but the state Senate acquitted him. Long-running securities fraud charges were also resolved without an admission of wrongdoing under an agreement requiring restitution and community service. More recently, his marriage collapsed amid allegations of infidelity, while fresh reporting has raised questions about his relationships with wealthy donors and businessmen. Paxton denies wrongdoing and has portrayed his legal and political troubles as efforts by establishment figures to destroy him. His supporters have largely stood by him, valuing his willingness to fight their political battles over questions about his personal conduct. That loyalty helped him defeat four-term incumbent senator John Cornyn by 28 percentage points in a Republican primary runoff in May after Trump threw his weight behind Paxton. It was a striking demonstration of how thoroughly Trump's movement has reshaped Texas Republican politics. by Moises Avila with Frankie Taggart in Washington (AFP)

items.originalTitle: The painstaking task of cataloguing the world's species
items.author: Estelle.Bronkhorst
items.title: The painstaking task of cataloguing the world's species
items.summary: The painstaking task of cataloguing the world's species Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 10:30 PARIS - A bumblebee-like insect that was last seen in France 150 years ago was spotted again in the Paris region in 2025. Had the creature, known by its scientific name Pocota personata, disappeared and returned after all those years? Or did it simply fly around unnoticed this whole time? The mystery illustrates the challenge facing scientists seeking to catalogue the world's biodiversity, as so much of nature remains poorly understood. The gap in scientific data on the state of species could feature prominently at the UN's COP17 biodiversity summit opening Monday in Armenia, where countries will take stock of progress in commitments to protect nature. In order to close that gap in France, the National Museum of Natural History (MNHN) and the National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) launched a project in June to build a database of the country's plants and invertebrates. "We know biodiversity is declining, but we are sometimes quite helpless when it comes to quantifying it due to a critical lack of data on the current and past monitoring of species," Rodolphe Rougerie, head of the Dynabiod project, told AFP. - Staggering unknown - The scale of the unknown is huge. A 2011 study estimated that 86 percent of terrestrial species and 91 percent of marine creatures had yet to be formally described. Even among identified species, their status is often poorly understood. In 2025, scientists had assessed the extinction risk of only about eight percent of known species, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature. The tools used to identify species include field observations. While spotting large mammals or certain birds can be relatively simple, the exercise gets trickier when it comes to smaller species, such as insects, fungi or microscopic organisms. The job can be painstaking. Every week, MNHN researcher Fanny Kratz checks large white tents that serve as insect traps at the Jardin des Plantes, a botanical garden in the heart of Paris, and 16 other sites. She then uses their DNA to fill gaps in the data. The task is "very, very long" and "very, very complicated", she said. A single trap can contain as many as 261 types of DNA, but those genetic traces do not necessarily correspond to 261 different species. And there are always a few "unknowns" -- DNA that does not match with anything in existing databases. - 'We are stuck' - "The difficulty with biodiversity is having reference databases that are rich enough ... so that field work or genetic identification can actually be effective," Kratz said. The smallest details can make all the difference when trying to identify a specimen, from the size of a leg to the shape of the wing. And there are relatively few experts in this field. Researchers often turn to citizen science, enlisting amateur naturalists and the public to put more eyes on the ground. But that cannot replace scientific expertise and can introduce biases. Observations tend to be concentrated in easily accessible locations while others remain unexplored. That is particularly true in tropical regions, where areas can be hard to reach and data is scarce despite their extraordinary biodiversity, Kratz said. While artificial intelligence can analyse enormous quantities of data, it is only as good as the information it has been trained on. "If we don't have the reference database, we're stuck," Kratz said. - Muddled message - It's not just the amount of data that matters. Scientists also need to be able to compare data collected in different places and at different times. Different monitoring methods can make that difficult. Rougerie said the result can be a muddled scientific picture. When data are sparse, scattered or collected using different methods, separate studies can sometimes reach conflicting conclusions about what is happening to the same species. That can, in turn, fuel claims that the biodiversity crisis is being exaggerated or is difficult to prove. Without reliable reference databases, Kratz said, "we cannot know what is happening ... what we are capturing or what is disappearing or not ... and therefore how to combat a possible decline or protect this or that species". by Delphine Paysant (AFP)

items.title: Mbappe hits two as Real Madrid rout Sevilla
items.summary: Mbappe hits two as Real Madrid rout Sevilla Estelle.Bronkhorst Mon, 10/19/2026 - 10:30 MADRID - Kylian Mbappe scored twice including one brilliant individual goal as Real Madrid thrashed Sevilla 4-1 on Sunday to climb into third in La Liga. Arda Guler, who was fortunate to avoid an early red card for an elbow, netted a spectacular opener before Mbappe's double and a rocket from Yan Diomande as Jose Mourinho side moved above Real Betis. Mbappe's first was a sensational strike, involving a roulette on the edge of Sevilla's box, and his second a chipped Panenka penalty. Champions Barca are six points ahead of Real Madrid before next weekend's Clasico at Camp Nou after thrashing Betis on Saturday, with Atletico Madrid second, sandwiched between Spain's giants. "We played a great game... we are a team and we work to improve, we've only been together for a very short time," Mourinho told Real Madrid TV. "It's hard to have the calm that other coaches enjoy at other clubs, given the scale of Real Madrid, but we're making the most of every minute we have." Mourinho lined up with Diomande on the left in place of suspended Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior, and brought Guler in as part of the midfield pivot. Vinicius's red card for hair-pulling last weekend provoked ire in the Spanish capital at officiating in Spain. Madrid fans at their Santiago Bernabeu stadium chanted and held up banners against La Liga president Javier Tebas, after he said the club's strategy of trying to discredit referees was similar to the techniques of Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels. Los Blancos and their new coach Mourinho have complained bitterly about Spanish refereeing in recent weeks, and more generally over the past two seasons, in which they have failed to win a major trophy. On this occasion it was Sevilla who had more to complain about in terms of officiating as Madrid eased to victory. A quiet start was disrupted when Madrid midfielder Guler appeared to elbow Sevilla's Peque, which went unpunished midway through the first half. "There's a match that's 11 against 11 where they deserve to win, without any doubt, but we were denied the chance to play another match," said upset Sevilla coach Luis Garcia Plaza. "We were denied the chance to play a match of 11 against 10. From there on I don't want to talk about the match anymore. We should have been playing 11 against 10 from the 25th minute." The coach said "maybe" Guler was not dismissed so Madrid did "not arrive nine points behind" Barca at the Clasico next weekend. Mourinho said he had seen no replays of the incident which proved Guler had elbowed Peque. Sevilla had resisted the probing of Madrid's attacking stars early on, but were undone by a moment of magic from Guler himself after 30 minutes. Jude Bellingham played the ball out to the flank where record signing Diomande received it and fed Guler on the edge of the box. The Turkish playmaker lofted a superb strike across Sevilla goalkeeper Odysseas Vlachodimos and into the top corner. - Mbappe skill - Mbappe came close to adding a second with a lightning-quick burst down the pitch, but his low effort was saved. The French superstar soon got his goal, one of the best of the season. Bellingham backheeled the ball into Mbappe's path and the forward produced a dazzling roulette turn into the area, before showing more skill to rapidly sidestep the goalkeeper and roll home. Sevilla complained that striker Robbie Ure was fouled in the build-up, to no avail. Mbappe extended the lead from the penalty spot after he went down under a light touch from Andres Castrin in the area. The forward, who hopes to be crowned the best player in the world at the Ballon d'Or ceremony later in October, dinked home his ninth league goal of the season. Sevilla pulled one back with a neat strike from Manuel Bueno, but there was no fightback on the cards. Ivorian winger Diomande thumped home from outside of the box for his second goal since joining this summer from RB Leipzig, Madrid's next opponents in the Champions League. Earlier, Real Sociedad rose to fifth with a thumping 5-2 win at bottom side Malaga, Celta Vigo defeated Alaves 2-1 and Osasuna beat Racing Santander 2-0. AFP
